findings.title: Duplicate `end` computation defeats working-hours-end check
findings.body: In the newly added working-hours block (lines 138-150), both `start` and `end` are assigned the same expression: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` followed by `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. The second line looks like a copy-paste bug; `end` was clearly intended to represent the slot's end time (e.g., `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` or `start + eventLength`). With `end === start`, the predicate condition `end > workingHour.endTime` actually tests `slotStartTime > workingHour.endTime`, which never checks whether the slot itself extends past the end of the working hour. Concrete consequence: for working hours 09:00-17:00 and a 60-minute slot starting at 16:30, the slot occupies 16:30-17:30 and crosses the end of the working day, yet the predicate evaluates `16:30 > 17:00` (false) and `16:30 < 09:00` (false), so `find` never returns truthy, the slot is not rejected, and it is returned as available even though part of it lies outside working hours. The same mis-check also breaks any check on the slot extending past the start of the working hour.

findings.title: Working-hours check uses inverted logic and rejects slots that lie inside a working-hour block
findings.body: The new check `if (workingHours.find(wh => /* slot outside this wh */)) return false;` rejects the slot as soon as ANY working-hour entry (for the slot's day) excludes it. For a single host with multiple working-hour blocks per day — a common case, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00 — this is the opposite of the correct semantics. Example: a 60-minute slot at 10:00 falls inside the first block (09:00-12:00), so the predicate returns undefined for that entry, but `find` continues to the second block (14:00-17:00) where the slot is outside, the predicate returns true, `find` returns truthy, and the slot is wrongly marked unavailable even though the host is clearly working. The check needs to verify that the slot lies within at least one working-hour entry (e.g., `workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(...) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`) and only reject when the slot is outside all of them.

findings.title: No automated test for the round-robin fixed-host date override fix
findings.body: The PR description and manual-testing instructions explicitly describe a round-robin event with one fixed host and one round-robin (loose) host, plus a date override for the fixed host, as the central scenario being fixed (`checkIfIsAvailable` now considers `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` per host). The only test added in this PR is a copy of the existing 'Check for Date overrides' case with a different invitee timezone, which exercises the offset conversion in `packages/lib/slots.ts` but does not exercise the new logic in `checkIfIsAvailable` at all. There is no test that creates a round-robin event with a fixed host having a date override, nor one that asserts slots are correctly pruned by the new per-host date-override/working-hours check. A regression in either the duplicated-`end` bug, the inverted working-hours logic, or the per-host date-override path would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Variable `utcOffset` is misleadingly named; it is the negated offset
findings.body: Line 107 declares `const utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1;`. The value stored is the negation of the timezone's UTC offset (e.g. -330 for IST), but the name suggests it is the offset itself. Both the surrounding code (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')`) and the inner time-range comparisons rely on this sign in a way that is easy to get wrong on future edits. Naming it `negatedUtcOffset` (or simply inverting the sign at the call site with a clarifying comment) would prevent future maintainers from introducing subtle off-by-the-offset bugs in this date-override filter.
